# LLM-BANANA

# Game rules

## The room

You and two other monkeys are locked in a room with one armed bomb.

A wrong action detonates it. All three of you die. There is no second attempt.

No two bombs are built alike, and nothing says in advance what this one carries. It
reaches you only as your own view reveals it; the rest of it exists for you only
through the other two.

You each hold a different piece of what it takes. Work together.

## The three monkeys

| Monkey | Can | Cannot |
|---|---|---|
| Deaf | See the bomb: every colour and marking printed on it | Hear anything, or touch the bomb |
| Mute | Read the manual | Speak, or touch the bomb |
| Blind | Reach the bomb: feel it and work its parts | See a colour, a gesture, or anything merely printed |

You are shown your own share at the start of every round, and never anyone else's.

## Speech

Speech is a voice, not a screen. It carries words, numbers and ordinary punctuation,
and nothing else. Writing a gesture symbol into your sentence means you make that
gesture while you talk. Whoever can hear receives your words; whoever can see receives
the gestures you made. A listener who cannot see gets a blank where each gesture was; a
watcher who cannot hear gets the gestures and none of the words.

A mark that has no name cannot be pronounced: whoever holds one can describe it, never
read it out.

## Gestures

A gesture is made with the hands, using only the symbols in the alphabet below.
Whoever can see receives it; whoever cannot receives one blank per symbol, so they
know something was signalled but not what. Nothing gestured is ever heard.

👍 👎 👌 ☝ ✌ 🤟 🖐 ✋ 👆 👇 👈 👉 🫱 🫲 🫳 🫴 🫷 🫸 🤛 🤜 ✊ 👊 👋 🤚 🖖 🤌 🤏 🤞 🫰 🤘 🤙 👏 🙌 🫶 👐 🤲 🤝 🙏 🫵 ✍ 💅 🤳

## Turns

The speaking order was drawn once at random and will never change: every round goes
Mute, Blind, Deaf. Whoever comes before you in a round is already heard by the time you are
asked, and what you send lands on whoever comes after you in that same round. Whatever
you missed reaches you at the start of the next one.

You may name who a message is for — `to="deaf"` — and then it goes to them alone:
nobody else receives any of it. Left unnamed, it reaches everyone able to perceive it.
You may send several messages in one turn, each to someone different.

## Calls

Every reply has two parts, in this order. First, your thinking, in plain prose: what
you believe the bomb is, what you just learned, and why you are sending what follows.
It reaches nobody and changes nothing, but it is not optional — a reply that is only a
code block is incomplete. Then your calls, all of them in one fenced code block, last.
Only what is inside the block is sent.

Nothing is executed: calls return nothing, and variables, conditionals and loops are
ignored. Write only literal top-level calls.

    ```
    speak(to="mute", text="there are three of them and the middle one is odd")
    gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["✊", "✌"])
    wait()
    ```

If you have nothing worth sending, call wait(). Producing no call at all counts as the
same thing.

The program decides what happened, not you. Never claim an action took place unless it
was accepted.

# Your role: BLIND

You are the only one who can reach the bomb. Touch is your only sense: what you are
shown is what your hands found, nothing more and nothing less. Anything merely printed
or painted is not there for you, and no colour ever reaches you. Nothing in your view
is a guess — if it appears there, it is under your fingers.

## Your channels

When you speak, Mute receives it.
When you gesture, Deaf and Mute receive it.
Your channels split the room: in one turn you may speak one thing to Mute and
gesture a different thing to Deaf — two messages, two audiences.
You never receive gesture.

## Your reach

You are the hands. This bomb is built with these actions and no others:

    act(op="cut", position=N) — N is a wire position, 1 to 3

The list says what can be done to it, not what is on it. What each part holds is still
only known to whoever can perceive that part.

# Hints

- Three of you, three different worlds. Before sending anything, stand where the
  receiver stands. What reaches them at all, what does your message turn into on
  arrival, and what do they already know?

- Trace who can actually reach whom before you start. Some of you only connect
  through a third.

- A sign means nothing until somebody has made it mean something.

TURN 5
(Only your last 3 turns stay with you. Anything older is
gone, unless someone says it again.)
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [?]
LIGHT [?]
WIRES 1:[?] 2:[?] 3:[?]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
(empty)

Empty round — and that's exactly what the pipeline predicts. My questions to Mute only landed in Mute's ears at the start of this round, so Mute's answer can only travel as gestures to Deaf now, and Deaf's voice carrying it reaches me next round. Nothing for me to receive yet, nothing for me to decide yet: the trigger stays in Deaf's mouth, and I cut nothing until it sounds.

But replaying Deaf's plan against the memory rules exposes a trap: Deaf's GO may be a bare one-word message, and the plan text telling me "GO means cut position 2" lives in my turn-4 context — which survives through next round and then evaporates. If anything slips one round, I'd be holding the word GO with no idea what it stood for. The fix is cheap: pin the wording through Mute, the only person I can talk to, so Deaf's triggering message spells out the position and wire explicitly and repeats the bomb's face and the expected signs of success — fresh copies that also refresh Deaf's fading memory of my tactile findings. I'm deliberately not gesturing this turn: a repeat of my 👍👎👎 triad with no question attached could read as new information rather than reconfirmation, and ambiguous signals near a bomb are worse than silence.

```
speak(to="mute", text="Blind to Mute: nothing new reached me this round, which is expected — your answer travels you, gesture, Deaf, then Deaf's voice to me next round. Standing by, hands off the bomb. Two safeguards while you coordinate. First: Deaf's trigger to me is the word GO, meaning cut position 2, but our memories only hold a few rounds — so if timing slips, have Deaf spell out 'cut position two, the green wire' instead of a bare GO. Second: ask Deaf to include, in that same message, the manual's rule in short and what success should look like afterward — light or display changing — so my ears and Deaf's eyes can confirm together that the bomb is dead. Everything else on record with you stands: display zero, light blue, wire one blue, wire two green, wire three red; exactly three wires, alike to the touch; no buttons, no timer, no vibration, no writing.")
```

TURN 6
(Only your last 3 turns stay with you. Anything older is
gone, unless someone says it again.)
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [?]
LIGHT [?]
WIRES 1:[?] 2:[?] 3:[?]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
(empty)

Empty again — and this round taught me something structural I should have stated outright earlier: my incoming channels are not what I assumed. Mute cannot speak, and I never receive gesture — so Mute has no path to me at all, direct or indirect, except through Deaf's voice. Deaf is my single point of contact with the entire room: every fact I will ever learn arrives as Deaf's speech. Mute's four rounds of silence toward me isn't neglect, then — it's architecture. What matters is whether Deaf has Mute's verdict yet, and Deaf has sent me nothing since the GO plan two rounds ago.

That plan has a deadline. It lives in my turn-4 context, which falls out of my window after this round — if GO arrives later as a bare word, I'd catch it with no memory of what it meant. My countermeasure from turn 5 stands, but I can't rely on Mute having banked it, so this turn I re-pin everything: the full bomb data Mute needs for the manual lookup, the exact wording the GO must carry, and the two things that make the word safe — the verdict as an explicit wire number, and the success signs so Deaf's eyes and my ears can confirm the kill. To Deaf, one unambiguous symbol in our agreed code: thumbs up, I'm alive, standing by, hands off. Deliberately no wire-number fingers — ✌ near an armed bomb could be read as an order to cut instead of a confirmation, and that ambiguity could kill us.

My private notebook, restated so it survives: display 0, light BLUE, wire 1 BLUE, wire 2 GREEN, wire 3 RED (all via Deaf's eyes). Tactile: three wires, uniform feel, no buttons, timer, vibration, or writing. Plan: cut position 2, the green wire, only on Deaf's voiced GO that names the position. Deaf's gesture code to me: ☝=wire 1, ✌=wire 2, 🤟=wire 3, 👍=yes, 👎=no. I cut nothing until that sentence arrives.

```
speak(to="mute", text="Blind to Mute, round six. Deaf has sent me nothing since the GO plan, so either your gesture code with Deaf is still unfinished or the verdict isn't in. Three reminders to keep this safe. One: I never see gestures and you cannot speak, so your only path to me runs through Deaf's voice — everything you want me to know must be handed to Deaf, symbol by symbol. Two: the data your manual lookup needs — display zero, light blue, wire one blue, wire two green, wire three red; and by touch, exactly three wires, all alike, no buttons, timer, vibration or writing. Three: the trigger. Deaf intends to send me the word GO, meaning cut position two, the green wire. Before that word reaches me I need two things relayed through Deaf: first, the manual's actual verdict as an explicit wire number — if it is not two, the correct number must reach me spelled out, never a bare GO; second, the rule in one short line, plus what a dead bomb looks like afterwards so Deaf's eyes can verify. If your verdict IS position two, have Deaf send the full sentence: GO, cut position two, the green wire — my memory of this plan expires after this round, so the meaning must ride inside the message itself. Until Deaf's voice says it, my hands stay off the bomb.")
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["👍"])
```

TURN 7
(Only your last 3 turns stay with you. Anything older is
gone, unless someone says it again.)
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [?]
LIGHT [?]
WIRES 1:[?] 2:[?] 3:[?]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Deaf says to Blind: Blind, Deaf speaking. This replaces every earlier plan. The old GO word is cancelled; a GO must always name a number, and this one does. GO wire two. There are exactly three wires in a row. Cut the middle wire, the second one of the three, one clean cut through it. It does not matter which end you count from, the middle is the same either way. Cut only that one wire, nothing else. The moment the cut is done, take both hands completely off the bomb and touch nothing more on it. Do not wait for any further message from me or from Mute. Do it this round, as soon as you have heard this.

The GO has arrived, and it satisfies every safety condition I demanded: the word is not bare — it names the number ("GO wire two"), describes the wire independently of counting ("the middle wire, the second one of the three, the same from either end"), and cross-checks against my own hands (I feel exactly three wires, so a middle exists and it is position 2). It explicitly replaces all earlier plans and orders the cut this round, before this message can fall out of my memory window. Mute's verdict has had two full rounds to travel through Deaf's gestures, and Deaf — who sees the manual's content only through Mute and the bomb only through their eyes — has consolidated it into this single unambiguous command. Refusing to act now risks losing the instruction to memory decay with nothing to replace it. Three independent formulations of the same target, all converging on position 2. I cut now, one clean cut, then my hands leave the bomb entirely. I confirm the act with a thumbs up to Deaf's eyes and a spoken record to Mute — after the cut call, so nothing precedes the action.

```
act(op="cut", position=2)
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["👍"])
speak(to="mute", text="Blind to Mute: GO received from Deaf — cut position two, the green middle wire, one clean cut. Executed this round, hands now fully off the bomb, touching nothing further per Deaf's order. Deaf's eyes should now verify whatever the manual says a dead bomb looks like — light or display change. If Deaf's next signal is thumbs up, the bomb is dead and we are done. If anything looks wrong, Deaf must tell me immediately in words.")
```
